source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization is Nearly Inevitable (in Linear Models)
source.authors: Scott Geng; Dutch Hansen; Jerry Li

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies weak-label supervised fine-tuning in a new linear logistic-regression setting, but evaluates student improvement with accuracy and cosine similarity rather than the original PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The study reports theoretical guarantees and simulation outcomes for weak-label fine-tuning. Figure-only gains are not assigned numerical values. Learning-rate sweeps are described as training setup, not outcome rows. The paper also reports that training too long hurts after gains peak; it does not state whether the student then falls below the weak teacher.
record.test_reason: The study proves and simulates weak-label SFT in linear logistic regression. A student that starts more accurate than its teacher (80% vs 60–75%) improves on its own accuracy, so it ends above the supervisor. This bears on V1, on V3's teacher-accuracy dependence, and on V5's sufficient conditions. PGR and a ground-truth ceiling are not computed.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that a capacity mismatch between student and teacher is not needed, contrary to prevailing theory. Teacher–student disagreement (uncorrelated errors) may suffice. Gains are small but non-trivial and require early stopping.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised fine-tuning on weaker-model pseudo-labels, but in synthetic linear logistic regression rather than pretrained frontier models; evaluates accuracy and cosine improvement, not PGR; relies on early stopping.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that weaker teachers yield smaller gains, and that further training after the peak hurts. The simulations report little apparent dependence of total gain on initial student norm.
record.problems: The empirical evidence is simulation-based in a single 100-dimensional Gaussian linear setting. Numerical gains are primarily shown in figures rather than stated in text; PGR is not calculated. There is no direct comparison of outcomes under different error-correlations, distribution shift, or alternative training losses.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result rows omitted. Learning-rate values are training setup, not outcomes.

untested.parts: PGR, comparison with a ground-truth-trained ceiling, and any setting where the student starts weaker than or equal to the teacher.
All parts: no auxiliary confidence loss, no ensembling, no loss variants.
Model size scaling, tasks (NLP, chess, reward modelling) and learned representations. Only teacher accuracy and initial student norm are varied, in d=100 Gaussian data.
Distribution shift, exploitation of unverifiable errors, and any experiment directly varying teacher–student error correlation.
All parts: no vision or other modality.

missing.what: The theory's condition (ii) requires the student and teacher to be poorly correlated in directions orthogonal to θ* (similar errors make ρ small); the text calls this necessary. The shared-pretraining run shows the correlations stay low. This bears on V4's 'gains shrink when models err alike', but only as an argued condition, never varied experimentally. No row records it.
missing.locator: Theorem 1.1 condition (ii); 'Non-aligned students and teachers' paragraph; Eq. (2); Section 3.2

record.verdict_notes: The student always starts more accurate than the teacher, so 'beats the supervisor' holds from step 0. The informative result is improvement over the student's own start, which is stronger than V1 and different from the original's PGR framing. All empirical evidence is figure-only, from d=100 Gaussian simulations. V4 is not given a verdict; its bearing is recorded under missing, since the paper argues the condition but does not test it.

versions.untested_parts: PGR is not calculated, and the paper does not report a general comparison against a strong model trained on true labels. Results are for linear logistic regression and test accuracy or cosine similarity.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, or loss-variant comparison.
No sweep over model sizes, tasks, modalities, or learned representations. The study varies teacher accuracy and initial student norm in a linear Gaussian task.
No distribution-shift test, exploitability test, or direct experiment varying similarity of teacher and student errors.
The theory guarantees student improvement under weak supervision, not that the student must outperform its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.

rows.subject: linear logistic regression student (student-teacher pair)
rows.size_stated: d-dimensional; d is not fixed in the theorem
rows.operation_detail: Theorem A.8 guarantees student cosine-similarity improvement after SGD fine-tuning on teacher pseudo-labels.

conditions.value: SGD; specified step size and batch-size conditions

rows.measure: Change in cosine similarity with the ground-truth classifier
rows.value: cosΣ(θ̂T, θ*) − cosΣ(θ0, θ*) ≳ α*; Theorem A.9 gives Δ := C2(ρ/(∥θ0∥ + 1 + ε))²
rows.uncertainty: Failure probability bounded as stated in Theorem A.8; Theorem A.9 also gives a failure-probability bound.
rows.note: A theoretical sufficient condition and guarantee for improvement. It does not itself guarantee that the student exceeds the teacher.
rows.check: This is a theorem giving sufficient conditions (ρ>0, approximate ellipticity, low teacher–student correlation orthogonal to θ*) for SFT on weak labels to improve the student. That is what V5 names, so link V5. The guarantee is improvement over the student's own start. It implies beating the supervisor only when the student starts stronger than the teacher, which holds in all the paper's simulations.

source_check.reason: R2–R4 characterize a predictor: norm changes learning dynamics while peak gains remain nearly unchanged. This answers V3's dependence question; it does not demonstrate incomplete weak-to-strong generalization. A shrinking lower bound is compatible with these gains.

source_check.notes: Theorem A.9 fixes β=1 and inherits nonnegative initial-alignment assumptions from Appendix A; its constants depend on covariance eigenvalues. Exact numerical gains are not reported for the simulation rows; approximately elliptical accuracy comparisons require the paper's additional regularity assumptions.

statements.correction: Gain peaks and then declines; authors state eventual convergence to teacher labels; finite-time post-peak accuracy relative to the teacher is not reported.
statements.problem: The linear-model description is accurate, but the challenges label is too broad for all training past the peak: declining performance does not establish finite-time failure to beat the teacher.

statements.correction: Guaranteed improvement decreases with initial norm; simulated total gains are nearly independent of norm; the bound does not capture that empirical behavior. Guarantee compares final and initial student cosine similarity and requires a prescribed finite training horizon.
statements.problem: A norm-dependent lower bound does not contradict simulated gains that are nearly independent of norm.
